name: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
aliases: respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn

clinicalPearls: A disease of surfactant deficiency affecting mainly preterm infants; incidence rises steeply as gestational age falls, being greatest below about 28 weeks.
Distress typically begins at or soon after birth with tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal recession, and cyanosis that worsen over the first hours to days.
Chest radiograph classically shows a diffuse fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) pattern with air bronchograms and low lung volumes.
Antenatal maternal corticosteroids given before anticipated preterm delivery accelerate lung maturation and markedly reduce incidence and severity.
Exogenous surfactant replacement, delivered into the airway, is a cornerstone of treatment and improves oxygenation and survival.
Early nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) helps maintain functional residual capacity and can reduce the need for intubation and mechanical ventilation.

Maternal diabetes, male sex, second-born twins, caesarean delivery without labour, and perinatal asphyxia increase risk, whereas chronic intrauterine stress and prolonged rupture of membranes may reduce it.
Untreated disease tends to worsen for about 2-3 days before recovery begins, often heralded by a spontaneous diuresis.
reference.pathophysiology: Immature type II pneumocytes produce insufficient pulmonary surfactant, so alveolar surface tension is high. This causes progressive diffuse atelectasis, reduced lung compliance, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia with acidosis follow, and pulmonary vascular resistance may remain elevated with right-to-left shunting. Epithelial injury and protein-rich exudate form the hyaline membranes that give the disease its historical name, further impairing gas exchange.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal pneumonia or early-onset sepsis (especially group B streptococcus)
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph to assess the reticulogranular pattern and lung volumes
Arterial or capillary blood gas to quantify hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis
Pulse oximetry and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
Blood culture and inflammatory markers when sepsis cannot be excluded
Echocardiography if congenital heart disease or pulmonary hypertension is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly escalating oxygen or ventilatory requirement
Sudden deterioration suggesting pneumothorax or other air leak
Persistent hypoxaemia despite surfactant and respiratory support (possible pulmonary hypertension)
Apnoea, bradycardia, or signs of impending respiratory failure
Hypotension and poor perfusion suggesting shock or sepsis
reference.prognosis: With antenatal steroids, surfactant, and modern respiratory support, survival is high, particularly in more mature preterm infants; outcome worsens with decreasing gestational age and with complications such as air leak, intraventricular haemorrhage, and progression to bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
pitfalls: Assuming RDS in a term or near-term infant without considering sepsis, aspiration, or cardiac causes
Over-oxygenation, which increases the risk of retinopathy of prematurity and oxidative lung injury
Delaying surfactant or CPAP in an infant who is deteriorating
Failing to recognise a tension pneumothorax as the cause of abrupt worsening
Not administering antenatal corticosteroids when preterm birth is anticipated
